title: Market Cycles: Bull Markets, Bear Markets, and How to Behave
content:
The stock market doesn't go up in a straight line. It moves in cycles — periods of rising prices followed by periods of decline, then recovery, and expansion again. Understanding market cycles helps investors avoid costly emotional decisions and stay on course toward long-term financial goals.

## The Four Phases of a Market Cycle

Market cycles generally move through four phases:

**1. Accumulation (Recovery)**: After a market bottom, prices are low and economic news is still bad. Smart 'contrarian' investors start buying because valuations are attractive. Volume is low; pessimism still dominates. This is the hardest phase to invest in because confidence is low.

**2. Markup (Bull Market)**: Economic conditions improve, corporate earnings rise, and investor confidence grows. More participants enter the market, pushing prices higher. This phase can last years — the longest US bull market ran from 2009 to 2020, an 11-year run with the S&P 500 gaining over 400%. Investor sentiment becomes increasingly optimistic, then greedy.

**3. Distribution (Market Top)**: Prices peak, volume stays high but increasingly driven by retail investors who have become euphoric. Insiders and institutional investors begin selling. Market tops are very hard to identify in real time — everyone feels great and 'this time is different' becomes a common rationalization.

**4. Markdown (Bear Market)**: Prices fall significantly, negative economic news accelerates the decline, and fear grips the market. Investors who bought near the top panic and sell, locking in losses. The cycle eventually reaches a new bottom, and accumulation begins again.

## Bull Markets

A **bull market** is defined as a period in which stock prices rise at least 20% from a recent low, sustained over at least two months. Bull markets are associated with strong economic growth, low unemployment, rising corporate earnings, and investor optimism.

**Notable bull markets**:
- **1990–2000**: 10-year dot-com bull run, S&P 500 gained ~415%
- **2003–2007**: Post-dot-com recovery, S&P 500 gained ~100%
- **2009–2020**: Post-financial crisis, the longest bull market in US history, S&P 500 gained ~400%+
- **2020–2021**: Brief but fierce pandemic recovery bull market

Historically, bull markets last longer and produce greater gains than bear markets cause losses — which is why long-term buy-and-hold investing works.

## Bear Markets

A **bear market** is defined as a 20% or greater decline from a recent peak, sustained over at least two months. Bear markets are typically associated with recessions, rising unemployment, falling corporate earnings, and investor pessimism.

**Notable bear markets**:
- **2000–2002**: Dot-com bust. NASDAQ fell ~78%; S&P 500 fell ~49%
- **2007–2009**: Financial crisis. S&P 500 fell ~57% peak to trough
- **2020**: COVID crash. S&P 500 fell ~34% in just 33 days (but recovered in months)
- **2022**: Rate hike bear market. S&P 500 fell ~25%; bonds fell too, an unusual double decline

Bear markets are painful but historically temporary. The average bear market lasts about 9–12 months, while the average bull market lasts 2.7 years or more.

## Market Corrections

A **market correction** is a decline of 10–20% from a recent high — less severe than a full bear market. Corrections are common and healthy — they shake out speculative excess and create buying opportunities.

On average, the US stock market experiences a 10%+ correction roughly once per year. They feel alarming in the moment but are entirely normal. A correction that continues past -20% becomes classified as a bear market.

## Recessions and Markets

A recession is typically defined as two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth. Recessions are often (but not always) accompanied by bear markets. Importantly, the stock market is a leading indicator — it typically starts falling several months before an official recession is declared, and starts recovering several months before the recession ends.

This lag is why trying to 'sell before the recession' and 'buy back when it's over' is so difficult — by the time the recession is officially declared, the market may already be recovering.

## How to Behave During Market Downturns

This is where most investors' returns diverge from the market's returns. The right behavior during a downturn:

**1. Don't panic-sell**: Selling during a crash locks in losses and means you'll likely miss the recovery. JP Morgan's annual study consistently shows that missing just the 10 best days in a 20-year period cuts your returns roughly in half.

**2. Keep investing (dollar-cost average)**: If you invest regularly, a market decline means your contributions buy more shares at lower prices — a genuine benefit. The worst thing you can do is stop investing when stocks are 'on sale.'

**3. Rebalance**: A market drop shifts your allocation (you now have less stocks relative to bonds). Rebalancing forces you to buy more stocks when they're cheap — the opposite of emotional investors who are selling.

**4. Check your allocation**: If a 30% drop causes you to lose sleep, your stock allocation is too aggressive for your risk tolerance. Consider whether your allocation was appropriate before the crash — not during it.

**5. Zoom out**: Bear markets look terrifying on a 1-year chart and completely insignificant on a 30-year chart. Time horizon is everything.

**6. Remember history**: Every bear market in history has eventually recovered and reached new all-time highs. The COVID crash — the fastest bear market in history — recovered in just 5 months.

The investor who stays the course through cycles consistently outperforms the investor trying to dodge every downturn.
